claims.text: Simultaneous wear–corrosion resistance in HEAs is governed by the ability to form and continuously regenerate a protective passive layer.
A nanocrystalline, chemically homogeneous, single-phase structure minimizes local galvanic gradients.
A nanocrystalline, chemically homogeneous, single-phase structure promotes rapid repassivation after mechanical damage.
The proposed initial material is a uniformly distributed nanocrystalline HEA consisting primarily of a single BCC or FCC solid solution.
Uniform elemental distribution impedes the formation of detrimental galvanic couples.
Lattice distortion and sluggish atomic diffusion are inherent characteristics of HEAs relevant to passive-layer regeneration.
Fresh surfaces created by abrasion quickly develop a stable, adherent passive oxide layer.
Dynamic repassivation minimizes corrosive elemental leaching.
Dynamic repassivation maintains high surface hardness and thereby improves wear resistance.
Phase segregation produces more pronounced micro-galvanic effects.
Coarse grains or phase segregation cause less effective repassivation.
Coarse-grained or phase-segregated HEAs consequently undergo higher combined degradation.
Under combined wear–corrosion conditions, the nanocrystalline homogeneous HEA will have a lower wear rate than the matched coarse-grained or phase-segregated baseline.
Under combined wear–corrosion conditions, the nanocrystalline homogeneous HEA will have a lower corrosion current density than the matched baseline.
The passive layer on the nanocrystalline HEA's wear track will remain intact and continuous because it rapidly regenerates after disruption.
The prediction should hold under moderately oxidizing conditions that permit protective-oxide formation.
The prediction may fail in an environment too reducing to form a passive layer or when mechanical damage outpaces repassivation.
The quantitative effects of grain size and elemental distribution on oxide stability and repassivation rate, including the failure threshold, are not established.
